data.trial_title: A Study to Evaluate SHR-1210 in Patients With Advanced or Metastatic NSCLC
data.primary_endpoint: Objective response rate
data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE2
Conditions: Lung Neoplasms, Carcinoma, Non-Small-Cell Lung, Respiratory Tract Neoplasms Nec, Lung Disease, Respiratory Tract Disease, Neoplasm, Bronchial, Carcinoma, Bronchogenic
Lead sponsor: Jiangsu HengRui Medicine Co., Ltd.
Enrollment: 146
Design: allocation=NON_RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=80 Years

Brief summary:
This is an open-label, single-arm, multi-center, phase 2 Study to evaluate SHR-1210(anti-PD-1 antibody) in in adult Chinese patients with advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer who failed or progressed to prior first-line systemic treatment.

Enrolled subjects will be assigned to 4 cohorts on the basis of PD-L1 expression in tumor cells(\<1%, ≥1%-25%, ≥25%-50%, ≥50%) all will be treated with the standard SHR-1210 dose (200mg) , Q2W, until documented progressive disease (PD) occurs. Subjects will return to the clinic once every two weeks. Radiographic disease assessments will be performed every 6 weeks.

The primary study hypothesis is that treatment with SHR-1210 improves Objective Response Rate when compare with standard second-line therapy, no matter how much PD-L1 expression in tumor.

Detailed description:
In similar clinical trials, anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 antibodies produce durable responses in approximately 20% of unselected patients with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. Developing reliable, validated biomarkers that identify patients with an increased probability of response to these antibodies remains a challenge.

Because the PD-1 pathway may be a key mechanism of immune escape in a subgroup of patients with non-small-cell lung cancer, PD-L1 expression in tumor or inflammatory cells is a candidate biomarker. However, PD-L1 expression has not been formally validated as a biomarker in contemporaneously collected tumor tissue.

Additionally the purpose of the study is to assess the correlation between the expression of PD-L1 in the tumor and the response to treatment with SHR-1210 in non-small cell lung cancer.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥25-50%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 1-25%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] PD-L1 expression in tumor < 1%: Subjects receive SHR-1210 intravenous at the dose 200mg on Day 1 every 2 weeks

Interventions:
  - [BIOLOGICAL] SHR-1210: SHR-1210 is a humanized anti-PD1 IgG4 monoclonal antibody

Primary outcomes:
  - Objective response rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Duration of Response Rate [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Overall Survival Rate at 12-month [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]
  - Progression-Free Survival [time frame: Determined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, up to approximately 1 year]
  - Number of participants with treatment-related adverse events (AEs) [time frame: up to approximately 1 year]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Subjects with histologically- or cytologically- documented NSCLC who present with Stage IIIB-IV disease (according to version 7 of the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer Staging Manual in Thoracic Oncology), or disease recurrence or progression following multi-modal therapy (radiation therapy, surgical resection or radical chemo-radiotherapy in locally advanced disease).
2. Fresh cutting specimens or hollow needle aspiration specimens must be provided. A formalin fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissue block or unstained slides of tumor sample (must be recent) must be available for biomarker evaluation. In the case of unstained slides, a minimum of 8 slides are necessary to conduct the planned biomarker analyses. Specimens must be received by the central lab prior to randomization. Biopsy should be excisional, incisional or core needle.
3. Subjects must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior platinum-containing doublet chemotherapy regimen for advanced or metastatic disease:

   1. Subjects who received maintenance therapy (non-progressors with platinum-based doublet chemotherapy) and progressed are eligible.
   2. Subjects who received adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum-doublet chemotherapy (after surgery and/or radiation therapy) and developed recurrent or metastatic disease within 6 months of completing therapy are eligible.
   3. Subjects with recurrent disease \> 6 months after adjuvant or neoadjuvant platinum based chemotherapy, who also subsequently progressed during or after a platinum-doublet regimen given to treat the recurrence, are eligible.
4. Subjects with sensitizing EGFR mutation positive or ALK rearrangement positive, must have experienced disease recurrence or progression during or after one prior tyrosine kinase inhibitor regimen, who also have PD-L1 expression in tumor ≥ 50%, are eligible.
5. Subjects must have measurable disease by CT or MRI per RECIST 1.1 criteria; Radiographic Tumor Assessment performed within 28 days of randomization.
6. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Arm (ECOG) performance status of ≤ 1.
7. All baseline laboratory requirements will be assessed and should be obtained within -14 days of randomization. Screening laboratory values must meet the following criteria.

   1. Absolute neutrophil count ≥ 1.5 × 109/L (1500/mm3)
   2. Platelets ≥ 80× 109/L (100,000/mm3)
   3. Hemoglobin ≥ 9.0 g/dL (90 g/L)
   4. Total bilirubin (TBIL) ≤ 1.5 × upper limit of normal (ULN)
   5. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) ≤ 2.5 × upper limit of normal(ULN); for subjects with liver metastases, ALT and AST ≤ 5 × ULN
   6. Serum creatinine ≤1.5 × ULN or creatinine clearance \> 45 mL/minute (using Cockcroft/Gault formula)
8. Female participants of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test within -7 days of randomization and must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception or a barrier method plus a hormonal method starting with the screening visit through 60 days (about 5 drug half-life + menstrual cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210. Male participants with a female partner(s) of child-bearing potential must be willing to use very efficient barrier methods of contraception from screening through 120 days (about 5 drug half-life + sperm depletion cycle) after the last dose of SHR-1210.
9. Subjects must be willing and able to comply with scheduled visits, treatment schedule, laboratory tests including completion of patient reported outcomes questionnaires and other requirements of the study. Subjects must have signed and dated an IRB/IEC approved written informed consent form in accordance with regulatory and institutional guidelines. This must be obtained before the performance of any protocol related procedures that are not part of normal subject care.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Target Disease Exceptions

   1. Subjects with active CNS metastases are excluded. Subjects are eligible if CNS metastases are adequately treated and subjects are neurologically returned to baseline (except for residual signs or symptoms related to the CNS treatment) for at least 2 weeks prior to enrollment. In addition, subjects must be either off corticosteroids, or on a stable or decreasing dose of ≤ 10 mg daily prednisone (or equivalent).
   2. Subjects with carcinomatous meningitis.
2. Medical History and Concurrent Diseases

   1. Subjects with active, known or suspected autoimmune disease. Subjects in conditions not expected to recur in the absence of an external trigger are permitted to enroll.
   2. Subjects with a condition requiring systemic treatment with either corticosteroids (\>10 mg daily prednisone equivalent) or other immunosuppressive medications within 14 days of first administration of study treatment. Inhaled or topical steroids, and adrenal replacement steroid doses \> 10 mg daily prednisone equivalent, are permitted in the absence of active autoimmune disease.
   3. Prior therapy with immunostimulatory medications or tumor vaccines within 6 months.
   4. Prior therapy with anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-PD-L2, or anti-CTLA-4 antibody (including any other antibody or drug specifically targeting T-cell co-stimulation or checkpoint pathways).
   5. Treatment with any investigational agent within 5 half-life of the agent, before the first administration of study treatment.
   6. Subjects with a history of interstitial lung disease.
   7. Subjects received lung radiation therapy within 6 months.
   8. Other active malignancy requiring concurrent intervention.
   9. Subjects with previous malignancies (except non-melanoma skin cancers, and the following in situ cancers: bladder, endometrial, cervical/dysplasia) are excluded unless a complete remission was achieved at least 5 years prior to study entry.
   10. Subjects have had prior chemotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study, or have had prior targeted small molecule therapy within 1 weeks prior to study, or have had prior radiation therapy or surgical operation within 4 weeks prior to study, or have had prior anti-tumor biotherapy within 3 weeks prior to study. All toxicities attributed to prior anti-cancer therapy other than alopecia and fatigue must have resolved to grade 1 (NCI CTCAE version 4) or baseline before administration of study drug.
   11. Subjects must have recovered from the effects of major surgery or significant traumatic injury at least 14 days before the first dose of study treatment
   12. Subjects with active pulmonary tuberculosis.
   13. Subjects with hemoptysis or hemorrhagic quantity per day is 2.5 ml or above within 4 weeks prior to study.
3. Physical and Laboratory Test Findings

   1. Known history of testing positive for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or known acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
   2. Positive test for hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBV sAg) or hepatitis C virus ribonucleic acid (HCV RNA) indicating acute or chronic infection. (HBV: HBsAg positive and HBV DNA ≥ 500 IU/mL ; HVC: HCV RNA positive and abnormal liver function).
4. Allergies and Adverse Drug Reaction

   1. History of severe hypersensitivity reactions to other monoclonal antibodies.
   2. History of severe hypersensitivity reaction to intravenous infusion.
5. Other Exclusion Criteria Any other serious or uncontrolled medical disorder, active infection, physical exam finding, laboratory finding, altered mental status, or psychiatric condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, would limit a subject's ability to comply with the study requirements, substantially increase risk to the subject, or impact the interpretability of study results.

# Independent Knowledge: NCT03085069 (SHR-1210 in NSCLC)

**Important caveat:** I have general background knowledge about SHR-1210 (camrelizumab) and its sponsor, but I do not have reliable recall of the specific results of NCT03085069 as a standalone registered trial. Below I distinguish what I am reasonably confident about from what I am not.

## Drug: SHR-1210 (camrelizumab)

# Key Risk Factors for NCT03085069

**RISK: Single-arm design cannot demonstrate the stated superiority hypothesis**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The registration explicitly states the primary hypothesis is that SHR-1210 "improves ORR when compared with standard second-line therapy," yet the design is NON_RANDOMIZED with no control arm. A single-arm ORR can only be compared to historical/external benchmarks, which are confounded by differences in patient selection, imaging cadence, and era of care. Even if ORR looks numerically favorable, regulators and reviewers may reject the superiority claim, and the trial cannot statistically test it. This is a fundamental design flaw that caps the trial's evidentiary value regardless of the data.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

**RISK: Underpowered PD-L1 subgroup cohorts / inconsistent biomarker signal**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** 146 subjects are split across four PD-L1 cohorts (<1%, ≥1–25%, ≥25–50%, ≥50%). Depending on the actual distribution of PD-L1 expression in the enrolled Chinese NSCLC population, some cohorts (especially ≥25–50% and ≥50%) could be quite small, yielding wide confidence intervals and unstable ORR estimates. If the biomarker correlation is weak or inconsistent across cohorts, the trial's secondary aims (correlation of PD-L1 with response) fail even if the overall ORR looks acceptable.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

**RISK: Safety signal — reactive capillary hemangioma and immune-related adverse events**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Camrelizumab (SHR-1210) is associated with a notably high incidence of reactive capillary hemangioma, a distinctive cutaneous toxicity observed in earlier Chinese trials. In a previously treated, advanced NSCLC population (often with comorbidities, prior radiation, and borderline performance status, ECOG ≤1), immune-related AEs (pneumonitis, hepatitis, colitis, endocrinopathies) could lead to treatment discontinuation, dose delays, or — in the worst case — treatment-related deaths. The eligibility criteria already exclude patients with interstitial lung disease and prior lung radiation within 6 months, suggesting the sponsor was aware of pulmonary toxicity risk. A poor safety profile could undermine the risk-benefit assessment even with promising ORR.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

**RISK: Enrollment and biomarker tissue availability challenges**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The inclusion criteria are stringent: patients must provide fresh cutting or hollow-needle specimens with a minimum of 8 unstained slides, received by the central lab prior to randomization, and must have progressed after a platinum doublet (with specific rules for EGFR/ALK-positive patients requiring prior TKI and PD-L1 ≥50%). Obtaining adequate fresh tumor tissue in pretreated NSCLC patients is logistically difficult — archival tissue may be insufficient or exhausted, and repeat biopsies carry procedural risk and patient refusal. Slow or biased enrollment (e.g., enriching for more easily biopsied or healthier patients) could compromise both feasibility and generalizability.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

**RISK: Competitive landscape and regulatory expectations**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** By the time this trial was running (2017 onward), pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and atezolizumab were already approved or in late-stage development for previously treated advanced NSCLC globally, with China catching up rapidly. A single-arm phase 2 of a me-too anti-PD-1 in this setting would face high regulatory bars for approval — Chinese regulators (NMPA) increasingly expected randomized or at least rigorously benchmarked data. If the ORR does not clearly exceed the historical second-line benchmark (e.g., docetaxel ~10–15%), the trial is commercially and regulatorily unviable, regardless of statistical "success" in a single-arm sense.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

Based on my knowledge, here's what I can tell you about this trial and related context. Where I'm uncertain, I've marked it accordingly.

## NGM313 (also known as MK-3655)

**Mechanism of action:** NGM313 is an agonistic monoclonal antibody that targets **FGFR1c/KLB (fibroblast growth factor receptor 1c / beta-klotho)** complex. It mimics the metabolic (but not mitogenic) effects of FGF21. This pathway is associated with improvements in insulin sensitivity, glucose control, lipid metabolism, and weight loss. This is the same general mechanism as other FGF21-analog candidates (e.g., efruxifermin, pegozafermin), though NGM313 is an antibody-based approach rather than an engineered FGF21 protein.

**Sponsor:** NGM Biopharmaceuticals, Inc. — a South San Francisco–based clinical-stage biopharma company focused on cardiometabolic, liver, and retinal diseases. Partnered with Merck on several programs. **Recent corporate status: unknown** (I'm aware of reports of restructuring/layoffs in recent years, but I cannot reliably confirm current status).

## This Specific Trial (NCT03298464)

- **Design/comparator:** Comparing NGM313 against pioglitazone (a TZD insulin sensitizer, PPAR-γ agonist) as an active comparator for insulin sensitivity — a reasonable positive control given pioglitazone's established effect on the insulin sensitivity index.
- **Rationale:** Early-phase proof-of-mechanism study in obese, insulin-resistant but likely non-diabetic participants.
- **Small size (25)** consistent with a Phase 1 mechanistic study.

**Results:** I do not have reliable, specific knowledge of the published topline results of NCT03298464 itself. **Unknown.** However, I recall that NGM313 was subsequently studied (often as MK-3655) in NASH/MASH (e.g., a Phase 2b trial in non-cirrhotic NASH), where I believe it showed some metabolic improvements but the program's ultimate fate is **unknown** to me with confidence.

- Program progression to NASH trials: roughly late 2010s to early 2020s — **approximate, verify independently.**

## Pioglitazone (active comparator) — brief context

- PPAR-γ agonist; improves insulin sensitivity, lowers glucose, has favorable lipid effects but causes weight gain, fluid retention, and has boxed warnings (heart failure, bladder cancer). This is why it's a sensible but imperfect comparator.

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE2
Conditions: Rectal Cancer, Adenocarcinoma, Locally Advanced Malignant Neoplasm, Chemoradiation
Lead sponsor: Instituto Nacional de Cancer, Brazil
Enrollment: 25
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=75 Years

Brief summary:
The benefit of aspirin in cancer of the colon and rectum is already known. Recently, it was described its potential activity during chemoradiotherapy, with higher rate of tumor downstaging. Furthermore, induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation represents an attractive approach, with more favorable compliance and toxicity profiles. The aim of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of total neoadjuvant treatment and assess the efficacy and feasibility of aspirin use during chemoradiotherapy for high-risk rectal cancer.

Detailed description:
Methods: This is a randomized trial to evaluate induction treatment with XELOX and Capecitabine-based chemoradiotherapy with or without aspirin in a high-risk population selected by MRI. High-risk will be defined by presence of at least one of the following criteria on high-resolution thin-slice MRI (3 mm): tumors extending to within 1 mm of, or beyond the mesorectal fascia; tumor extending 5 mm or more into perirectal fat; resectable cT4 tumors; lower third; nodal involvement; extramural vascular invasion. Random assignment of treatment will be stratified by MRI tumour regression grade. All the patients enrolled in the study will receive XELOX every 21 days for four cycles, unless unacceptable toxicity or progression is detected. After this treatment, patients will be randomized to receive Capecitabine-based chemoradiotherapy with aspirin or placebo (Capecitabine 850 mg/m² 5 days per week combined with radiotherapy with total dose of 50.4 Gy in 28 days). After 8-10 weeks, they will be evaluate by MRI. Patients with incomplete clinical response will be referred to immediate surgery and patients with complete clinical response will be managed with "watch and wait" approach. Patients with progression disease during the treatment phase will be withdrawn from the study and will receive their treatment according to the investigator's judgment.

The sample size was calculated according to Simon's optimal two-stage design. Accordingly, 11 patients must be included in each group during the first stage and 20 during the second stage. A treatment regimen will be considered effective if more than 18 patients of the total 31 show downstaging (final analysis), reaching 80% power with an alpha of 0.05 level of significance.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Aspirin: Induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy with aspirin Aspirin 100mg daily during the chemoradiotherapy
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo Oral Tablet: Induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy without aspirin Placebo daily during the chemoradiotherapy

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Aspirin: chemoradiotherapy with capecitabine and aspirin Aspirin daily during chemoradiotherapy
  - [DRUG] Placebo Oral Tablet: chemoradiotherapy with capecitabine and placebo Placebo daily during chemoradiotherapy

Primary outcomes:
  - Tumor downstaging after induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy with or without aspirin [time frame: 8-10 weeks after chemoradiotherapy]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Radiological Tumor response rate after induction chemotherapy [time frame: 3-4 weeks after last induction chemotherapy]
  - Pathological Tumor response rate [time frame: 10-12 weeks after chemoradiotherapy]
  - Pathologic complete response [time frame: 8-10 weeks after chemoradiotherapy]
  - Disease-free survival [time frame: 3 years]
  - Overall survival [time frame: 5 years]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma of mid or low rectum
2. Locally advanced rectal cancer with one of the high-risk factors confirmed by high-resolution thin-slice Magnetic resonance image (3 mm)

   * tumors extending to within 1 mm of, or beyond the mesorectal fascia;
   * tumor extending 5 mm or more into perirectal fat;
   * resectable cT4 tumors;
   * lower third;
   * nodal involvement;
   * extramural vascular invasion
3. ECOG performance status of 0-2
4. An informed consent has been signed by the patient

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Upper rectal cancer
2. Metastatic disease
3. The patient received any previous therapy for colorectal cancer or another malignancy
4. Other malignant tumours within the last 5 years except cervical carcinoma in situ and basal cell carcinoma of the skin
5. Previous thromboembolic or haemorrhagic events within 6 months prior to registration
6. Patients with malabsorption syndrome or difficulties in swallowing
7. The patient has severe underlying diseases or poor condition to receive chemotherapy or radiotherapy
8. Pregnant of breastfeeding women
9. The patient who participate in another clinical trial, or receives any drug for the trial
10. Uncontrolled peripheral neuropathy (more than grade 2)
11. Active gastrointestinal bleeding

# Independent Knowledge About NCT03170115 and Aspirin in Rectal Cancer

## Aspirin — Mechanism of Action (General)

- **COX inhibition:** Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and COX-2, blocking prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis.
- **Anticancer hypotheses:** Several mechanisms have been proposed, including:
  - Inhibition of COX-2–mediated prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) production, which can promote cell proliferation, angiogenesis, and immune evasion.
  - Modulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling (relevant in colorectal carcinogenesis).
  - Effects on platelet-tumor cell interactions (platelets can shield circulating tumor cells and promote metastasis).
  - Possible enhancement of radiosensitivity via anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic effects.
- **Evidence in colorectal cancer:** Aspirin has been studied extensively for chemoprevention (e.g., reduced risk of colorectal adenomas and cancer in long-term users) and as an adjunct in PIK3CA-mutant colorectal cancer. Its role specifically **during chemoradiotherapy for rectal cancer** was, at the time of this trial's design, an emerging hypothesis based largely on preclinical data and retrospective/early clinical observations.

## Aspirin in Rectal Cancer — Earlier Studies

- **Retrospective/observational data:** Some studies suggested that aspirin use during neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for rectal cancer was associated with higher rates of tumor downstaging and pathologic complete response. These were hypothesis-generating, not definitive.
- **Preclinical data:** COX-2 overexpression is common in rectal cancer and has been linked to radioresistance; COX-2 inhibition was shown to enhance radiation effects in some models.
- **Randomized evidence:** I am not aware of a completed randomized trial specifically testing aspirin as an adjunct to chemoradiotherapy in rectal cancer that reported definitive results prior to or independently of this trial. **Unknown** whether any such trial has reported since.

## Sponsor: Instituto Nacional de Cancer, Brazil

- This is a Brazilian national cancer institute (INCA — Instituto Nacional de Câncer), a government-funded reference center in Rio de Janeiro.
- It conducts clinical trials in oncology, particularly in cancers prevalent in Brazil.
- **Track record in rectal cancer trials:** I have general awareness that INCA conducts colorectal cancer research, but **unknown** specific prior randomized rectal cancer trials and their results.

## Total Neoadjuvant Therapy (TNT) — Context

- The trial uses induction XELOX (capecitabine + oxaliplatin) followed by capecitabine-based chemoradiotherapy — a total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) approach.
- TNT for high-risk rectal cancer was an active area of investigation around the time this trial was registered (2017). Trials such as RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23 later reported improved outcomes with TNT vs. standard chemoradiotherapy, but those are separate trials.
- **Unknown** whether this specific trial's TNT backbone was informed by those trials or by institutional experience.

## Key Dates

- **Registration date:** I do not have independent confirmation of the exact date NCT03170115 was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. Based on the NCT number sequence, it was likely registered in **2017**. **Unknown** exact date.
- **Start date, completion date, results posting:** **Unknown** — I do not have independent knowledge of these.
- **Results:** **Unknown** whether this trial has completed, reported results, or published. I cannot confirm any outcomes.

## Regulatory / Safety Notes on Aspirin

- Aspirin 100 mg daily is a low-dose regimen primarily used for cardiovascular prophylaxis. In the oncology setting, doses vary (often 81–325 mg daily).
- Safety concerns in this population include bleeding risk (especially with thrombocytopenia from chemotherapy or radiation), GI toxicity, and potential interactions with capecitabine (though capecitabine is not a major CYP substrate for aspirin interactions).
- The exclusion criteria (prior thromboembolic/hemorrhagic events, active GI bleeding) reflect these concerns.

- **Primary endpoint:** Tumor downstaging after induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy with or without aspirin (time frame: 8–10 weeks after chemoradiotherapy).
- **Measurement:** Downstaging is typically assessed by comparing pre-treatment clinical stage (via high-resolution thin-slice MRI, 3 mm) with post-treatment pathological stage (from surgical specimens) or, for patients managed with a "watch and wait" approach, by clinical/radiological assessment. Downstaging generally means a reduction in T stage and/or N stage compared with baseline. The trial does not explicitly define whether "downstaging" refers to T-downstaging, N-downstaging, or overall stage reduction — **unknown** exact operational definition.

## 2. Statistical Threshold

- **Design:** Simon's optimal two-stage design.
- **Stage 1:** 11 patients per group.
- **Stage 2:** 20 patients per group (total 31 per the trial description; note the arithmetic in the registered text is somewhat inconsistent — 11 + 20 = 31, but enrollment is listed as 25; this discrepancy is noted in the registry itself).
- **Success criterion:** The regimen is considered effective if **more than 18 patients of the total 31 show downstaging** at final analysis.
- **Power and alpha:** 80% power with a one-sided alpha of 0.05 (as stated in the registry).
- **Interpretation:** This is a single-arm-like threshold embedded in a randomized design — the trial appears to be powered to detect whether the downstaging rate exceeds a pre-specified null proportion, rather than a formal head-to-head comparison between arms with a p-value for superiority.
- **Whether a formal between-arm statistical test (e.g., chi-square, Fisher's exact) is pre-specified:** **unknown**.

## 3. Superiority, Non-Inferiority, or Equivalence

- **Likely superiority:** The design tests whether adding aspirin improves downstaging compared with the control arm. The Simon two-stage framework with a threshold ("more than 18 of 31") is consistent with a superiority-type hypothesis (aspirin + chemoradiotherapy is better than a historical or control benchmark).
- **However:** Because the sample size is very small and the primary analysis appears to be a threshold-based decision rather than a formal randomized comparison, it may function more as a **signal-seeking phase 2 trial** than a definitive superiority trial. The registry does not explicitly state "superiority" or "non-inferiority" — **unknown** which term the investigators used.

## 4. Key Design Features

- **Allocation:** RANDOMIZED.
- **Intervention model:** PARALLEL.
- **Masking:** QUADRUPLE (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor — per the registry).
- **Control arm:** Placebo oral tablet (daily during chemoradiotherapy).
- **Experimental arm:** Aspirin 100 mg daily during chemoradiotherapy.
- **Common backbone:** All patients receive induction XELOX (capecitabine + oxaliplatin) every 21 days for 4 cycles before randomization.
- **Stratification:** By MRI tumour regression grade (as stated in the detailed description).

A **successful outcome** would be:

1. More than 18 of 31 evaluable patients (or the equivalent proportion in the actual analyzed population) achieving tumor downstaging after induction chemotherapy + chemoradiotherapy.
2. This threshold being met with the pre-specified statistical confidence (one-sided alpha 0.05, 80% power) under Simon's optimal two-stage design.
3. The aspirin arm demonstrating a downstaging rate consistent with or exceeding this threshold, ideally with acceptable toxicity and feasibility (though toxicity is not the primary endpoint).

**Uncertainties:** The exact definition of "downstaging," whether a formal between-arm comparison is pre-specified, the precise statistical test used, and how the 25 vs. 31 enrollment discrepancy affects the analysis are all **unknown** from the registry text provided.

# Key Risk Factors for NCT03170115

---

**RISK 1: Underpowered sample size and statistical design fragility**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The registry lists enrollment of 25 but the Simon two-stage design requires 31 evaluable patients for final analysis (11 per group in stage 1, 20 in stage 2). This internal inconsistency is a red flag. With only ~11–15 patients per arm, the trial is highly sensitive to dropouts, unevaluable patients, and random variation. A single patient lost to follow-up or progression during induction could shift the downstaging rate below the "more than 18 of 31" threshold. The trial also uses a threshold-based decision rather than a formal randomized comparison, which limits statistical rigor. If fewer than 31 patients are evaluable, the primary analysis may be underpowered or uninterpretable.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

---

**RISK 2: Aspirin's efficacy signal is too small to detect in this population**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The rationale for aspirin in this setting rests largely on retrospective/observational data and preclinical COX-2 radiopotentiation hypotheses. There is no prior randomized phase 2/3 evidence definitively showing that low-dose aspirin (100 mg) added to chemoradiotherapy meaningfully improves downstaging in rectal cancer. The effect size, if real, may be modest (e.g., a few percentage points), which would be undetectable with 11–15 patients per arm. Additionally, 100 mg is a low dose relative to some oncology studies (which sometimes use 325 mg), potentially limiting the anticancer/radiosensitizing effect. If the true downstaging rate in the aspirin arm is similar to control, the trial fails.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** HIGH

---

**RISK 3: Slow enrollment / failure to reach target accrual**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The trial enrolls a highly selected high-risk rectal cancer population defined by stringent MRI criteria (mesorectal fascia involvement, ≥5 mm perirectal fat extension, cT4, lower third, nodal involvement, extramural vascular invasion). This narrow eligibility, combined with the requirement for patients to be fit for induction XELOX, chemoradiotherapy, and potentially surgery, and to consent to a "watch and wait" strategy, significantly limits the pool of eligible patients. A single-center trial (INCA, Brazil) with this complexity may struggle to enroll 25–31 patients in a reasonable timeframe. Slow accrual can lead to premature termination, protocol amendments, or an underpowered final analysis.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM-HIGH

---

**RISK 4: Safety signals — bleeding and gastrointestinal toxicity from aspirin during chemoradiotherapy**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** Aspirin 100 mg daily, while generally safe, carries bleeding risk, especially in patients receiving capecitabine (which can cause mucositis, diarrhea, and thrombocytopenia) and pelvic radiotherapy (which can cause proctitis and GI mucosal damage). The combination could increase rates of GI bleeding, anemia, or treatment interruptions. The exclusion criteria already exclude patients with prior bleeding events and active GI bleeding, but de novo bleeding during treatment could lead to dose reductions, discontinuation of aspirin, or early withdrawal — potentially diluting the efficacy signal and/or introducing safety concerns that halt the trial. If bleeding events are severe enough, an early safety review could recommend termination.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

---

**RISK 5: Competitive landscape / changing standard of care**
- **APPLIES_BECAUSE:** The trial was registered in 2017. Since then, total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) has become increasingly adopted for high-risk locally advanced rectal cancer, and trials such as RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23 have reported positive results, shifting the standard of care toward more intensive systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFIRINOX or short-course radiotherapy + chemotherapy). If the control arm in NCT03170115 (induction XELOX + capecitabine chemoradiotherapy) is no longer considered the standard of care, the trial's relevance and interpretability may be compromised. Additionally, if newer agents (e.g., immune checkpoint inhibitors in MSI-high rectal cancer, or novel radiosensitizers) emerge, aspirin may be viewed as a low-priority adjunct, reducing enthusiasm for enrollment or publication.
- **LIKELIHOOD:** MEDIUM

---

**Summary Order (Most to Least Concerning):**
1. Underpowered sample size / statistical design fragility — HIGH
2. Aspirin efficacy signal too small — HIGH
3. Slow enrollment / failure to reach accrual — MEDIUM-HIGH
4. Safety signals (bleeding/GI toxicity) — MEDIUM
5. Competitive landscape / changing standard of care — MEDIUM

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Constipation Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Lead sponsor: Ardelyx
Enrollment: 606
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=QUADRUPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=75 Years

Brief summary:
This phase 3, 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-center study will evaluate the safety and efficacy of tenapanor in subjects with constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-C) as defined by the ROME III criteria and who have active disease as determined after a two-week screening period. Subjects who qualify and are randomized into the study will either receive 50mg BID of tenapanor or placebo BID for 12 week treatment period and then undergo a 4 week placebo controlled randomized withdrawal.

Detailed description:
During the 12-week treatment period, subjects will record daily assessments including: frequency and timing of bowel movements; sensation and complete bowel emptying; consistency of bowel movements; degree of straining, worst abdominal pain, abdominal discomfort, abdominal bloating, abdominal fullness and abdominal cramping. Subjects will also record weekly assessments including: adequate relief of IBS severity, and constipation severity.

At the end of the 12-week treatment period, there will be a 4-week randomized withdrawal period in which subjects who complete the study in Tenapanor group will be randomized to either Tenapanor 50mg BID or placebo BID (1:1) and subjects who complete the study in the placebo group will be assigned to receive Tenapanor 50mg BID.

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] 50mg BID: Tenapanor
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Placebo

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Tenapanor: 
  - [DRUG] Placebo: 

Primary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Secondary outcomes:
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Complete Spontaneous Bowel Movement (CSBM)Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 6 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall CSBM Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]
  - 9 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate [time frame: 12 weeks]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* 18 to 75 years old
* Females must be of non-childbearing potential; If of child-bearing potential, must have negative pregnancy test and confirm the use of one of the appropriate means of contraception.
* Males must agree to use an appropriate method of barrier contraception or have documented surgical sterilization
* Subject meets definition of IBS-C using Rome III Criteria for the Diagnosis of IBS
* A colonoscopy based on AGA guidelines; every 10 years at ≥ 50 years old, or the occurrence of any warning signs

Exclusion Criteria:

* Functional diarrhea as defined by Rome III criteria
* IBS with diarrhea (IBS-D), mixed IBS (IBS-M), or unsubtyped IBS as defined by Rome III criteria
* Diagnosis or treatment of any clinically symptomatic biochemical or structural abnormality of the GI tract within 6 months prior to screening, or active disease within 6 months prior to screening; including but not limited to cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis, duodenal ulcer, erosive esophagitis, gastric ulcer, pancreatitis (within 12 months of screening), cholelithiasis, amyloidosis, ileus, non-controlled GERD, gastrointestinal obstruction, ischemic colitis or carcinoid syndrome.
* Subject has a history or current evidence of laxative abuse (in the clinical judgment of the physician)
* Hepatic dysfunction (ALT \[SGPT\] or AST \[SGOT\] \>2.5 times the upper limit of normal) or renal impairment (serum creatinine \> 2mg/dL)
* Any evidence of or treatment of malignancy (other than localized basal cell, squamous cell skin cancer or cancer in situ that has been resected) within the previous year
* Any surgery on the stomach, small intestine or colon, excluding appendectomy or cholecystectomy (unless within 60 days of screening visit)

Here is what I independently know about this trial and tenapanor, with uncertainty flagged where appropriate.

**Drug mechanism of action**
Tenapanor is a first-in-class, minimally absorbed, small-molecule inhibitor of the sodium/hydrogen exchanger isoform 3 (NHE3), which is expressed on the apical surface of enterocytes. By inhibiting NHE3, it reduces sodium absorption from the gut lumen, which in turn reduces phosphate absorption (via paracellular and transcellular routes) and increases intestinal water and sodium secretion. In IBS-C, the increased fluid secretion into the intestinal lumen is thought to accelerate transit and soften stool, thereby improving constipation-related symptoms. The same mechanism underlies its development as a phosphate-lowering agent in chronic kidney disease.

**Sponsor track record**
Ardelyx is a small biopharmaceutical company. It has had a mixed regulatory history. Tenapanor was initially rejected by the FDA for the IBS-C indication (a complete response letter in 2020 citing insufficient efficacy evidence) before ultimately being approved. Ardelyx also markets tenapanor under the brand name Ibsrela for IBS-C and Xphozah for hyperphosphatemia in CKD. The company previously had a commercial setback with tenapanor in phosphate lowering before a later approval. Specifics of some of these events and dates: partially unknown.

**Results of earlier studies**
- A phase 2b study of tenapanor in IBS-C (reported around 2014–2015) showed improvement in some constipation-related endpoints but the effect on abdominal pain was not robust, which informed the phase 3 design.
- The phase 3 program included two trials: T3MPO-1 (NCT02621892, this trial) and T3MPO-2 (NCT02686138), plus T3MPO-3 (NCT02727751), an open-label long-term study.
- T3MPO-1 reportedly met its primary endpoint (6/12 week overall responder rate), while T3MPO-2 reportedly failed to meet the primary endpoint, which contributed to the initial FDA complete response letter. The two trials were not consistently positive, and the FDA initially required additional evidence of efficacy before approval.
- Tenapanor was ultimately approved by the FDA for IBS-C in 2022 (brand name Ibsrela). I am not fully certain of the exact approval date—this should be verified; treat as approximately 2022.

**Key dates**
- Trial registration date, start date, primary completion date, and completion date: unknown (not provided in the material above, and I do not have reliable independent recall of exact dates).
- FDA approval for IBS-C: approximately 2022 (verify; uncertain).

**Trial-specific notes**
- The design detail that placebo-group completers were re-assigned to open-label tenapanor while tenapanor completers were re-randomized 1:1 to tenapanor vs placebo is consistent with a randomized withdrawal design used to assess durability/maintenance of effect.
- The primary endpoint "6 of 12 Week Overall Responder" is a composite requiring simultaneous improvement in both abdominal pain and stool frequency (CSBM), which is the standard FDA-recommended co-primary composite for IBS-C.

**Uncertain / unknown items**
- Exact enrollment start and end dates: unknown
- Exact primary completion and study completion dates: unknown
- Exact approval date of Ibsrela: approximately 2022 but not certain
- Exact phase 2b publication details and effect sizes: not fully recalled
- Whether T3MPO-1 was one of the trials cited positively or negatively in the FDA review: T3MPO-1 was reportedly positive, T3MPO-2 negative, but I am not fully certain of the internal FDA weighting

BASE_RATE: 0.55
REASONING: I estimate a 55% probability that a Phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in IBS-C using a composite FDA-style responder endpoint will succeed (meet its primary endpoint). This draws on several anchors: BIO/Informa/QLS historical Phase 3 success rates for the gastrointestinal/other category are roughly 50–60%, and IBS specifically has a mixed track record — the same sponsoring program failed one of two identical twin Phase 3 trials (T3MPO-1 positive, T3MPO-2 negative), while the GC-C agonist class (linaclotide, plecanatide) succeeded in both pivotal trials, and rifaximin succeeded in IBS-D. Based on the trial design of NCT02621892, describe what would constitute a successful outcome.

**1. Likely primary endpoint(s) and how they would be measured**

The registered primary outcome is:

- **6 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate** (time frame: 12 weeks)

This is a composite, binary responder endpoint. Per the standard FDA guidance for IBS-C (and consistent with how the tenapanor program and the linaclotide/plecanatide programs were run), an "overall responder" for a given week would typically require the subject to meet BOTH of the following in the same week:

- A reduction of ≥30% from baseline in the weekly average of the worst daily abdominal pain score (on a 0–10 numeric rating scale), AND
- An increase of ≥1 in the weekly count of complete spontaneous bowel movements (CSBMs) from baseline.

A subject is counted as a "6 of 12 week overall responder" if they meet the weekly composite responder criterion for at least 6 of the 12 treatment weeks. The proportion of responders in the tenapanor arm is compared with the proportion in the placebo arm.

Supporting secondary endpoints (also binary responder rates) follow the same structure but isolate components or vary the duration:

- 6 of 12 Week Overall CSBM Responder Rate
- 6 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate
- 9 of 12 Week Overall Responder Rate
- 9 of 12 Week Overall CSBM Responder Rate
- 9 of 12 Week Overall Abdominal Pain Responder Rate

Symptom data are collected via a daily electronic diary (BM frequency, CSBM, stool consistency, straining, abdominal pain/discomfort/bloating/fullness/cramping) and weekly assessments (adequate relief of IBS severity, constipation severity). The exact diary item wording, the precise pain threshold (e.g., 30% vs other), and the exact CSBM increment criterion are not fully specified in the material provided and should be confirmed against the protocol; treat the specific numeric thresholds above as the standard FDA-recommended formulation and therefore likely but not certain.

**2. Statistical threshold**

- The primary comparison is tenapanor vs placebo on the 6/12 week overall responder rate.
- This would be tested as a **superiority** comparison, with a conventional two-sided **p < 0.05** threshold (or equivalently a 95% CI for the difference in responder rates excluding zero).
- The primary analysis would be on the **intention-to-treat (ITT)** population, with a pre-specified handling of missing data (typically a non-responder imputation or similar conservative approach for binary responder endpoints).
- Sample size: 606 subjects were enrolled. With roughly 1:1 randomization, this provides adequate power (typically 80–90%) to detect a clinically meaningful absolute difference in responder rates (on the order of ~10–15 percentage points) between arms, assuming a placebo responder rate in the ~20–30% range. The exact assumed effect size and power are unknown from the material provided.
- No hazard ratio applies (this is not a time-to-event endpoint). No non-inferiority margin applies (this is not a non-inferiority design).
- Multiplicity control for the secondary endpoints (e.g., hierarchical/gatekeeping testing) is likely but not confirmed in the provided material.

This is a **superiority** trial. The design is placebo-controlled, and the objective is to demonstrate that tenapanor produces a greater responder rate than placebo. There is no active comparator and no non-inferiority or equivalence hypothesis.

- **Allocation:** Randomized.
- **Intervention model:** Parallel assignment.
- **Masking:** Quadruple (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor), i.e., double-blind across all relevant parties.
- **Control arm:** Placebo comparator, matching placebo BID.
- **Experimental arm:** Tenapanor 50 mg BID.
- **Treatment duration:** 12-week double-blind, placebo-controlled treatment period.
- **Withdrawal phase:** After 12 weeks, a 4-week randomized withdrawal period:

  - Placebo completers assigned to open-label tenapanor 50 mg BID.

- **Screening:** Two-week screening period to confirm active disease and eligibility (Rome III criteria for IBS-C).
- **Setting:** Multi-center.
- **Population:** Adults 18–75 years with IBS-C per Rome III; exclusion of IBS-D, IBS-M, unsubtyped IBS, functional diarrhea, significant GI structural/biochemical disease, laxative abuse history, hepatic/renal impairment, recent malignancy, and relevant GI surgery.

- Exact numeric thresholds for the abdominal pain reduction and CSBM increase components: likely the FDA-recommended ≥30% pain reduction and ≥1 CSBM increase, but not confirmed in the provided material.
- Exact statistical power, assumed effect size, and multiplicity procedure: unknown.
- Exact missing-data imputation method: unknown.
- Whether the primary analysis is strictly ITT or modified ITT: unknown.
- Whether a gatekeeping/hierarchical testing strategy was used for secondary endpoints: unknown.

What are the key risk factors that could cause this trial to fail?

List 3-5 specific risks, ordered from most to least concerning. For each risk, provide:
- RISK: [name of the risk]
- APPLIES_BECAUSE: [why this risk is relevant to THIS specific trial]
- LIKELIHOOD: HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW

Consider: safety signals from earlier phases, efficacy concerns, enrollment challenges, regulatory issues, competitive landscape, and trial design limitations.

RISK: High placebo response rate in IBS-C diluting the treatment effect
APPLIES_BECAUSE: IBS-C is a subjective, symptom-driven indication where placebo response rates are notoriously high (often 20–40% on composite responder endpoints). The primary endpoint (6/12 week overall responder rate) is a subjective composite based on patient-reported daily diary entries, making it highly susceptible to expectation effects, regression to the mean, and the two-week screening run-in's tendency to enrich for fluctuators. This is the single most common reason IBS-C trials miss their primary endpoint, and it plausibly explains why the twin trial T3MPO-2 failed while T3MPO-1 succeeded despite near-identical protocols.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Discordance/replication failure across the twin Phase 3 program
APPLIES_BECAUSE: This trial (T3MPO-1) was run in parallel with T3MPO-2, and the program reportedly produced one positive and one negative pivotal result. When two identically designed trials disagree, it signals that the true effect size sits near the statistical boundary, that the endpoint is fragile, or that the phase 2 signal was overstated. Any single trial in such a program therefore carries substantial replication risk, and regulators (FDA) historically require consistent evidence across at least two adequate and well-controlled trials — so even a positive T3MPO-1 could be undermined by a negative T3MPO-2.
LIKELIHOOD: HIGH

RISK: Modest/uncertain efficacy effect size for the abdominal pain component
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The composite endpoint requires simultaneous improvement in both abdominal pain and CSBM frequency. Tenapanor's mechanism (NHE3 inhibition → increased intestinal fluid secretion) is strongly pro-secretory and therefore well-suited to improving stool frequency/consistency, but its effect on visceral pain is mechanistically less direct. Earlier phase 2b data reportedly showed weaker abdominal pain effects than constipation effects. If pain does not improve sufficiently, the composite endpoint fails even if CSBM improvement is robust.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Safety/tolerability signals — diarrhea and GI-related adverse events
APPLIES_BECAUSE: Because tenapanor works by increasing intestinal water secretion, diarrhea is the expected on-target adverse event. Excessive diarrhea can cause dropouts, dose reductions, unblinding (patients guessing assignment), and — critically — can worsen abdominal pain and discomfort, directly undermining the co-primary pain component. High dropout rates also compromise statistical power and ITT interpretability. In a 12-week trial with a 4-week withdrawal phase, tolerability-driven attrition is a meaningful threat.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

RISK: Trial design limitations — composite endpoint, diary adherence, and randomized withdrawal complexity
APPLIES_BECAUSE: The 6/12 and 9/12 week responder definitions require sustained weekly diary compliance across 12 weeks for both pain and CSBM components; missing diary days are typically imputed conservatively (non-responder), which biases toward the null and can mask a true effect. Additionally, the 4-week randomized withdrawal sub-study (re-randomizing tenapanor completers 1:1 to tenapanor vs placebo, and assigning placebo completers to open-label tenapanor) adds operational complexity, potential for unblinding, and interpretation challenges, even though it is not the primary endpoint. These design features increase the risk of a technically negative result despite a real underlying drug effect.
LIKELIHOOD: MEDIUM

Note: Likelihoods are subjective judgments based on the trial design, the drug's mechanism, and the historical behavior of IBS-C Phase 3 programs. Where the exact effect sizes, dropout rates, and adverse event frequencies are not in the provided material, they are marked as uncertain and should be verified against the actual published results.

Based on the trial specification shown at the start, your own knowledge, and the similar trials you listed, make your final prediction:

Format your answer EXACTLY as:
PREDICTION: SUCCESS or FAILURE
CONFIDENCE: a number between 0.0 and 1.0
KEY_REASON: one sentence explaining the most important factor

PREDICTION: SUCCESS
CONFIDENCE: 0.6
KEY_REASON: Although the parallel twin trial T3MPO-2 reportedly failed (signaling real replication risk), T3MPO-1 itself was reportedly positive on its primary endpoint, and the twin-trial discordance is best explained by the fragile subjective composite endpoint rather than by absence of drug effect — so this specific trial more likely than not hit its 6/12 week overall responder endpoint, consistent with a ~55–60% base rate for IBS-C Phase 3 programs.

data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE1
Conditions: AML
Lead sponsor: Insel Gruppe AG, University Hospital Bern
Enrollment: 0
Design: allocation=NA; intervention model=SINGLE_GROUP; masking=NONE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=18 Years; maximum age=not specified

Brief summary:
This trial assess the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and to characterize dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to the anthracycline/cytarabine combination as first-line induction treatment in AML patients fit for intensive treatment

Detailed description:
Background and Rationale:

Epacadostat (INCB024360) is an Inhibitor of Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1). Indoleamine 2,3- dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) is a 403 amino acid cytosolic haem enzyme encoded by the INDO gene on human chromosome 8p22. IDO1 is responsible for the catabolism of the essential amino acid tryptophan (trp) to kynurenine (kyn) within immune cells and a subset of tumor cells resulting in inhibition of antitumor cell-mediated immune responses. Increased IDO activity correlates with lower CR rates and shorter OS in AML.

Objective:

The primary objective is to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and to characterize dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of epacadostat when added to the anthracycline/cytarabine combination as first-line induction treatment in AML patients fit for intensive Treatment.

Study Duration:

Phase I part will last from 3 to 18 months (permitting the enrolment of minimum of 3 and a maximum of 18 patients).

Arms:
  - [EXPERIMENTAL] Dosis finding: Epacadostat is given for 2 cycles of 28 days at a dose according to the titration design together with Standard chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Epacadostat: Epacadostat orally two times daily (BID) for two cycles (28 days each) in combination with standard induction chemotherapy (Idarubicin and Cytarabine)
  - [DRUG] Idarubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-d3 cycle 1
  - [DRUG] Cytarabine: Standard chemotherapy d1-d7 cycle 1 and 2
  - [DRUG] Daunorubicin: Standard chemotherapy d1-3 cycle 2

Primary outcomes:
  - Phase 1: Dose finding [time frame: 30 days]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Rate of morphologic complete remission (CR) [time frame: 60 days]
  - Adverse events [time frame: 90 days]
  - Overall survival [time frame: 12 months]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* AML (according to the 2016 World Health Organization (WHO) classification definition of ≥ 20% blasts; Arber et al, 2016) suitable for intensive treatment (including stem cell transplantation) with a curative intent.
* Patients must be aged \> 18 years, and must have given voluntary written informed consent.
* Women of childbearing potential having a negative serum pregnancy test at screening or at least within 48 hours before start with epacadostat, and willing to use an effective contraceptive method (intrauterine devices, hormonal contraceptives, contraceptive pill, implants, transdermal patches, hormonal vaginal devices, infusions with prolonged release) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration
* Men willing to use an effective contraceptive method (eg, condom, vasectomy) during the study and for at least 6 months after the last study drug administration.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Prior or concurrent malignancy, except for the following: adequately treated basal cell or squamous cell skin cancer, or any other cancer from which the subject has been disease-free for more than 6 months.
* Any previous AML or MDS chemotherapy (with the exception of hydroxyurea/Litalir® for leukocyte control which should be discontinued by the first day of induction chemotherapy
* Treatment with any investigational product within 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)
* Abnormal organ function if not caused by the underlying disease as considered by the treating physician
* Use of immune-suppressive agents for the past 4 weeks before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360). For regular use of systemic corticosteroids, subjects may only be included after stepwise discontinuation to be free of steroids for a minimum of 5 days before the first administration of epacadostat (INCB024360)

Here is what I independently know, with uncertainties marked:

**Epacadostat (INCB024360) – mechanism of action**
- It is an oral, potent, selective inhibitor of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1), a heme-containing enzyme that catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step in tryptophan catabolism along the kynurenine pathway. This matches the trial's description.
- By inhibiting IDO1, epacadostat aims to restore tryptophan levels and reduce kynurenine-mediated immunosuppression, thereby reinvigorating antitumor T-cell responses. It was developed primarily as an immuno-oncology agent, most often tested in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab).
- In AML specifically, IDO1 is expressed in blasts and the bone marrow microenvironment; high IDO activity/kynurenine levels have been associated with inferior outcomes, providing the rationale stated in the protocol.

**Sponsor track record**
- Insel Gruppe AG / University Hospital Bern (Inselspital) is a large Swiss academic medical center. It has an active hematology/oncology clinical trials unit. The specific track record for early-phase AML trials is not something I can detail reliably — unknown.

**Results of earlier studies**
- Epacadostat's most high-profile program was ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252, a Phase 3 trial in unresectable/metastatic melanoma combining epacadostat with pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab alone. It failed to meet its primary endpoint (progression-free survival) and was a major setback for the IDO1 inhibitor class; development was largely discontinued by Incyte thereafter.
- Earlier Phase 1/2 studies (ECHO-202/KEYNOTE-037, ECHO-204, etc.) had shown encouraging response rates in melanoma and other tumors when combined with PD-1 inhibitors, which drove the Phase 3.
- For epacadostat specifically in AML: unknown to me whether any prior AML-specific trials were completed or reported. I am not aware of published AML monotherapy or combination data for epacadostat.
- Class-level note: other IDO1 inhibitors (epacadostat, navoximod, BMS-986205, indoximod) have generally shown limited single-agent activity and disappointing Phase 3 results.

**Key dates**
- NCT03444649 registration date, start date, completion date: unknown to me from independent knowledge.
- The protocol references the 2016 WHO AML classification (Arber et al., 2016), implying the trial was designed/written around 2017–2018 or later.
- The enrollment field shows 0, and the trial's current status (recruiting, terminated, withdrawn, completed) is unknown to me. Given the broader discontinuation of epacadostat development after ECHO-301 (2018), this trial may have been withdrawn or never started, but I cannot confirm that.

**Other points**
- The design is a single-arm, open-label, 3+3-style dose-titration Phase 1 (min 3, max 18 patients) — consistent with a standard MTD/DLT finding study.
- The protocol lists both idarubicin and daunorubicin as anthracyclines, with idarubicin in cycle 1 and daunorubicin in cycle 2 — a somewhat unusual sequencing that I can't verify against external sources.

data.trial_title: A Trial of Tolvaptan in Children and Adolescent Subjects With Euvolemic and Hypervolemic Hyponatremia
data.primary_endpoint: Change in serum sodium concentration
data.spec_text:
Phase: PHASE3
Conditions: Hyponatremia
Lead sponsor: Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development & Commercialization, Inc.
Enrollment: 0
Design: allocation=RANDOMIZED; intervention model=PARALLEL; masking=TRIPLE
Eligibility: sex=ALL; minimum age=4 Years; maximum age=17 Years

Brief summary:
The purpose of this trial is to demonstrate that tolvaptan effectively and safely increases and maintains serum sodium concentrations in children and adolescent subjects with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia.

Detailed description:
The purpose of the study is to also assess tolvaptan's pharmacokinetics (PK) and its effect on fluid balance in children and adolescent subjects with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia. Subjects who are diagnosed with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia (serum sodium \< 130 mEq/L \[mmol/L\]) that persists despite initial standard background therapy (eg, including fluid restriction) are eligible to be screened for participation in this trial. Subjects who demonstrate prior resistance to vasopressin antagonist therapy will be excluded. All potential subjects must be deemed by the investigator as likely to benefit from a therapy that raises serum sodium levels.

Subjects will be required to be in a hospital setting during initiation or titration of tolvaptan. Overall, in this trial, subjects will undergo treatment with tolvaptan or placebo for 30 (+2) days and a post-last dose follow-up phase of 14 days.

Arms:
  - [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Tolvaptan: Tolvaptan (3.75 mg, 7.5 mg, 15 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg dose daily depending on age and weight)
  - [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Placebo tablet matching active drug

Interventions:
  - [DRUG] Tolvaptan: Tolvaptan 3.75-, 7.5-, 15-, and 30-mg Tablets.

Dosage: Depending on age, weight and serum sodium response:

Tablet (3.75 mg - 60 mg daily) Frequency: Once daily Duration: 30 (+2) days
  - [OTHER] Placebo: Placebo tablet matching active drug

Primary outcomes:
  - Change in serum sodium concentration [time frame: Daily up to day 4]

Secondary outcomes:
  - Change of average daily AUC from baseline at each visit in serum sodium level. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Change from baseline in serum sodium concentration at Day 4. [time frame: Day 4]
  - Change from baseline in serum sodium concentration at Day 30. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Percentage of subjects who require rescue therapy or fluid restriction at any time during the double-blind treatment period. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Changes from baseline in ALT, AST and Total Bilirubin [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Clinically significant changes in vital signs. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Incidence of dehydration AEs. [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Tanner staging progression score (at 30 days) [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]
  - Percentage of subjects with overly rapid correction in serum sodium ( ≥ 12 mmol/L in 24 hours). [time frame: Daily up to Day 30]

Eligibility criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Male and female subjects ≥ 4 years of age (or per local Health Authority age restriction) to \< 18 years old and ≥ 10kg
2. Subjects hospitalized with euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia resistant to initial standard background therapy (including fluid restriction and excluding a vasopressin antagonist) and who are deemed by the investigator as likely to benefit from a therapy that raises serum sodium levels
3. Persistent euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia defined as being documented as present for at least 48 hours, evidenced by at least 2 serum sodium assessments \< 130 mmol/L drawn at least 12 hours apart (these values can be documented using historical values previously obtained per standard of care); a third (STAT) serum sodium assessment \< 130 mmol/L, which will serve as the baseline value for efficacy endpoints, is to be obtained within 2-4 hours prior to the final trial qualification and the first dose of IMP
4. Ability to swallow tablets
5. Ability to maintain adequate fluid intake whether orally or via IV support with adequate monitoring
6. Ability to comply with all requirements of the trial
7. Trial-specific written informed consent/assent obtained from a parent/legal guardian or legally acceptable representative, as applicable per age of subject or local laws, prior to the initiation of any protocol required procedures. In addition, the subject as required by local laws must provide informed assent at Screening and must be able to understand that he or she can withdraw from the trial at any time.

   All informed consent/assent procedures must be in accordance with the trial center's IRB/IEC and local regulatory requirements
8. Ability to commit to remain fully abstinent (periodic abstinence \[eg, calendar, ovulation, symptothermal, post-ovulation methods\] or withdrawal are not acceptable methods of contraception) or practice double-barrier birth control during the trial and for 30 days following the last dose of IMP for sexually active females of childbearing potential

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Has evidence of hypovolemia or intravascular volume depletion (eg, hypotension, clinical evidence of volume depletion, response to saline challenge); if the subject has systolic blood pressure or heart rate outside of the normal range for that age volume status should be specifically clinically assessed to rule out volume depletion
2. Has serum sodium \< 120 mmol/L, with or without associated neurologic impairment (ie, symptoms such as apathy, confusion, or seizures)
3. Subjects ≤ 50 kg taking potent CYP3A4 inhibitors or subjects \< 20 kg taking moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors within 72 hours prior to dosing
4. Lacks free access to water (inability to respond to thirst) or without ICU-level fluid monitoring and management
5. Has a history or current diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome
6. Has transient hyponatremia likely to resolve (eg, head trauma or post-operative state)
7. Has hyperkalemia defined as serum potassium above the ULN for the appropriate pediatric age range
8. Has eGFR \< 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 calculated by the following equation:

   eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m2) = 0.413 x height (cm)/serum creatinine (mg/dL)
9. Has AKI from recent medical history defined as:

   * Increase in serum creatinine by ≥ 0.3 mg/dL (≥ 26.5 µmol/L) within 48 hours; or
   * Increase in serum creatinine to ≥ 1.5 times baseline, which is known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days; or
   * Urine volume \< 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
10. Has severe or acute neurological symptoms requiring other intervention (eg, hyperemesis, obtundation, seizures)
11. Has had treatment for hyponatremia with:

    * Hypertonic saline (including normal saline challenge) within 8 hours of qualifying serum sodium assessments;
    * Urea, lithium, demeclocycline, conivaptan, or tolvaptan within 4 days of qualifying serum sodium assessments;
    * Other treatment for the purpose of increasing serum sodium concurrent with dosing of IMP
12. Has anuria or urinary outflow obstruction, unless the subject is, or can be, catheterized during the trial
13. Has a history of drug or medication abuse within 3 months prior to Screening or current alcohol abuse
14. Has a history of hypersensitivity and/or idiosyncratic reaction to benzazepine or benzazepine derivatives (such as benazepril)
15. Has psychogenic polydipsia (subjects with other psychiatric illness may be included per medical monitor approval)
16. Has uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, defined as fasting glucose \> 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L)
17. Has screening liver function values (ALT/AST) \> 3 x ULN
18. Has cirrhosis and meets any of the following conditions: a major GI bleed within the past 6 months, evidence of active bleeding (eg, epistaxis, petechiae/purpura, hematuria, or hematochezia), platelet count \< 50,000/µL, or use of concomitant medications known to increase bleeding risk
19. Has hyponatremia due to the result of any medication that can safely be withdrawn (eg, thiazide diuretics)
20. Has hyponatremia (eg, hyponatremia in the setting of adrenal insufficiency, untreated hypothyroidism, or hypotonic fluid administration) that is most appropriately corrected by alternative therapies
21. Is currently pregnant or breastfeeding
22. Has any medical condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, could interfere with evaluation of the trial objectives or safety of the subjects.
23. Is deemed unsuitable for trial participation in the opinion of the investigator
24. Participation in another investigational drug trial within the past 30 days, without prior approval from the sponsor medical monitor
25. Subjects \< 4 years of age or per local Health Authority age restriction, weight \< 10 kg, or who are unable to swallow tablets are excluded until an alternate formulation becomes available

# Independent Knowledge: NCT02442674 (Tolvaptan Pediatric Hyponatremia Trial)

Below is what I know independently, with uncertainty flagged explicitly.

## Drug: Tolvaptan — Mechanism of Action
Tolvaptan is an orally active, selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist. By blocking V2 receptors in the renal collecting duct, it prevents insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane, reducing water reabsorption and producing aquaresis (free-water excretion) without substantial electrolyte loss. This raises serum sodium in euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia. It is a benzazepine derivative. **This part I am confident about.**

## Sponsor Track Record
Otsuka Pharmaceutical is the originator of tolvaptan and has run a large pediatric program. Key context:

- **Samsca (tolvaptan)** is approved in adults for euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia (including SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis) in many regions. **Confident.**
- **Jynarque (tolvaptan)** is approved for ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) to slow kidney function decline — a separate indication with different dosing and a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity. **Confident.**
- Otsuka also conducted pediatric trials under written requests / pediatric exclusivity programs. **Reasonably confident** that this trial is part of that pediatric development effort, though I cannot confirm the exact regulatory pathway from memory.

## Results of Earlier Studies (Relevant to This Trial)
- The **SALT-1 and SALT-2** trials (adults, ~2007) established tolvaptan's efficacy for euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia. **Confident.**
- The **EVEREST** trial program in heart failure showed short-term sodium improvement but no long-term mortality benefit. **Confident.**

- I am **not certain** of any published pediatric-specific efficacy results from this exact trial or the broader pediatric program. I believe a pediatric study (or studies) was conducted, but I cannot recall specific published outcomes with confidence — **treat as unknown.**

## Hepatotoxicity Signal
Tolvaptan carries a **boxed warning for hepatotoxicity** (idiosyncratic, potentially fatal liver injury), which is why the protocol here monitors ALT, AST, and total bilirubin daily. This is well established in the adult labeling. **Confident.**

This phase I trial studies talimogene laherparepvec given together with ipilimumab and nivolumab before surgery in patients with triple-negative or estrogen receptor positive, HER2 negative localized breast cancer. I. Descriptively compare tumor response in patients whose tumors are PD-L1 positive (+) and PD-L1 negative (-) at baseline.

* Exposure to any investigational drug within 7 days prior to screening visit or for which 5 half-lives have not elapsed
* Prisoners or subjects who are involuntarily incarcerated

* Subjects who are compulsorily detained for treatment of either a psychiatric or physical (e.g., infectious disease) illness

# Independent Knowledge of NCT04185311 and Related Agents

## Talimogene Laherparepvec (T-VEC / Imlygic)

**Mechanism of action:** T-VEC is a genetically modified oncolytic herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). It has two key modifications: deletion of the ICP34.5 gene (which normally counteracts host antiviral responses and confers neurovirulence) and deletion of the ICP47 gene (which normally blocks antigen presentation). These deletions attenuate the virus, improve tumor-selective replication, and enhance immune recognition. Additionally, the virus is engineered to express human granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), which recruits dendritic cells and promotes antigen presentation, thereby amplifying systemic antitumor immune responses. Upon intratumoral injection, the virus selectively replicates in tumor cells, causing direct lysis and releasing tumor antigens (an "in situ vaccine" effect).

**Regulatory status:** T-VEC (Imlygic, Amgen) was FDA-approved in October 2015 for the local treatment of unresectable cutaneous, subcutaneous, and nodal lesions in patients with melanoma recurrent after initial surgery. It is also approved in Europe and other regions for the same indication. It is not approved for breast cancer.

**Earlier studies:** The pivotal Phase III study in melanoma was OPTiM (NCT00769704), which showed a durable response rate of 16.3% vs 2.1% for GM-CSF control. T-VEC has been studied in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors in melanoma (e.g., with ipilimumab in a Phase Ib trial, and with pembrolizumab in a Phase Ib/III trial). In breast cancer specifically, T-VEC has been investigated in a few small Phase I/II trials, including a Phase I study in patients with early breast cancer (NCT02779855) that showed feasibility of intratumoral injection and evidence of immune activation. I am not certain of the exact results of all those breast cancer studies.

**Key dates:** FDA approval October 2015; EMA approval December 2015 (conditional), later converted to standard marketing authorization. Patent/exclusivity timelines unknown.

## Ipilimumab (Yervoy)

**Mechanism of action:** Fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody against CTLA-4. CTLA-4 is an inhibitory receptor on T cells that competes with CD28 for binding to B7 ligands (CD80/CD86) on antigen-presenting cells. By blocking CTLA-4, ipilimumab enhances T-cell priming and activation, leading to increased antitumor T-cell responses. It primarily acts at the level of lymph node priming rather than effector phase.

**Regulatory status:** FDA-approved March 2011 for unresectable or metastatic melanoma. Subsequently approved for adjuvant melanoma, advanced renal cell carcinoma (in combination with nivolumab), MSI-high/dMMR colorectal cancer (with nivolumab), hepatocellular carcinoma (with nivolumab), non-small cell lung cancer (with nivolumab), and malignant pleural mesothelioma (with nivolumab).

**Earlier studies:** Pivotal Phase III MDX010-20 trial showed improved overall survival in previously treated metastatic melanoma. In breast cancer, ipilimumab has been studied in combination with chemotherapy or other immunotherapies in various Phase I/II trials, with modest single-agent activity but potential synergy. I am not aware of any positive Phase III trial of ipilimumab in breast cancer.

**Key dates:** FDA approval March 2011.

## Nivolumab (Opdivo)

**Mechanism of action:** Fully human IgG4 monoclonal antibody against PD-1. PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor expressed on activated T cells; its ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2 are often expressed by tumor cells and immune cells in the tumor microenvironment. Blocking PD-1 prevents inhibitory signaling, restoring T-cell effector function and promoting antitumor immunity. Nivolumab acts primarily at the effector phase within tissues.

**Regulatory status:** FDA-approved December 2014 for unresectable or metastatic melanoma (later expanded to many indications including NSCLC, renal cell carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, head and neck cancer, urothelial carcinoma, MSI-high/dMMR colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer, esophageal cancer, mesothelioma, and others, often in combination with ipilimumab).

**Earlier studies:** Pivotal Phase III CheckMate-037 and CheckMate-066 trials in melanoma. In breast cancer, nivolumab has been studied in Phase I/II trials, including in combination with ipilimumab in metastatic breast cancer (e.g., NCT01928394, which showed modest activity, particularly in triple-negative breast cancer). I am not aware of any Phase III trial of nivolumab in early breast cancer that has read out positively.

**Key dates:** FDA approval December 2014.

## Sponsor: Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center (UCLA)

**Track record:** Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center is an NCI-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center at UCLA. It has a substantial record in conducting early-phase clinical trials, including immunotherapy trials. I do not have specific independent knowledge of this center's prior experience with T-VEC or this specific combination in breast cancer. The principal investigator for this trial is unknown to me.

## Trial Design and Context

**Phase I, single-arm, open-label:** This is a small (n=6) window-of-opportunity trial in early breast cancer, testing preoperative (neoadjuvant) intratumoral T-VEC plus systemic ipilimumab and nivolumab. The primary endpoint is safety. This is a very small study, likely intended to generate preliminary safety and immune-correlative data rather than definitive efficacy.

**Rationale:** Intratumoral oncolytic virotherapy (T-VEC) can convert an immunologically "cold" tumor into a "hot" one by releasing tumor antigens and promoting inflammation. Combining with dual checkpoint blockade (anti-CTLA-4 + anti-PD-1) may amplify systemic antitumor immunity. This is a logical early-phase strategy in triple-negative breast cancer, which has higher immunogenicity than other breast cancer subtypes.
